# The Museum of Almost

The museum occupied a former railway station on a street that no longer led anywhere important. Its clock had stopped at eleven minutes past four, though whether morning or afternoon was disputed by the staff. Above the entrance, where the destination board had once hung, someone had painted:

**THE MUSEUM OF ALMOST**

Below that, in smaller letters:

**Please do not complete the exhibits.**

Mara arrived on a Tuesday carrying her father’s unfinished map.

She had rolled it into a cardboard tube intended for a fishing rod. On the bus, she kept it upright between her knees, feeling foolish whenever anyone glanced at it. She had inherited plenty of things that could be sold, donated, or placed in cupboards. The map was different. It seemed to require a decision that she had neither the information nor the temperament to make.

At reception, a man was repairing the cuff of his sweater with green thread.

“Donation?” he asked.

“Possibly.”

“That’s the usual kind.”

He finished a stitch before looking up. His name badge said ELIAS. Beneath the name, in a much smaller font, was the word TEMPORARY.

“How temporary?” Mara asked.

“Seventeen years so far.”

She smiled politely.

“No,” he said, “that really was meant to be funny.”

He gave her a visitor’s badge and pointed toward the old departures hall.

“Have a look around. People sometimes change their minds.”

“About donating?”

“About what they’ve brought.”

Then he returned to the cuff, which appeared to have been repaired many times in many different colors.

***

The first gallery contained objects that looked ordinary until you read their labels.

A blue woolen sleeve lay in a glass case.

**One sleeve of a sweater intended for a younger brother. Knitter learned, after completing the sleeve, that the brother disliked wool. Neither mentioned this again.**

Beside it stood a model ship with no rigging.

**Abandoned upon discovery that the builder preferred making small wooden crates. See adjacent collection.**

The adjacent collection consisted of thirty-seven excellent crates.

Mara had expected sorrow. There was sorrow, certainly, but it had been mixed with embarrassment, impatience, changing interests, and practical inconvenience.

One case displayed a university application stained with tea. Another held three pages of a detective novel in which everyone introduced in the first chapter had already been murdered. A wedding seating chart bore so many alterations that it resembled a military campaign conducted entirely through resentment.

In the center of the room stood a wooden chair with three legs.

The label read:

**Not an artistic statement.**

Mara laughed aloud.

An elderly woman studying a nearby cabinet nodded in approval, as if Mara had finally understood the rules.

“My husband made that,” she said.

“The chair?”

“He was going to even up the legs. You know how that goes.”

“Did he make furniture?”

“Only the once.”

The woman moved on to a display of abandoned crossword puzzles.

Mara looked again at the chair. Someone had polished its seat. Someone had thought it worth preserving, despite its inability to perform the single task expected of it.

***

She found Elias in the former ticket office, eating an orange over a wastebasket.

“My father made maps,” she said.

“Professionally?”

“He inspected drainage systems professionally.”

“That can involve maps.”

“Not these.”

She removed the paper from its tube. It resisted being flattened, lifting at the corners like something trying to get comfortable.

Elias cleared his desk.

The map showed a coast intricately indented with bays and estuaries. Mountains crowded the north. There were roads, railway lines, municipal boundaries, reservoirs, and symbols explained in a meticulous legend. Small towns possessed names such as Bellweather, Lower Orison, and Saint Venn.

Along the western edge, everything stopped.

The coastline ended in open paper. Three roads approached the margin and vanished. A river flowed from a blank space without any indication of its source.

“He worked on it for twenty years,” Mara said.

Elias bent closer.

“Was he writing a book?”

“No.”

“Designing a game?”

“Not that I know of.”

“Did he talk about it?”

“He said the western districts were difficult.”

Elias nodded with a seriousness that irritated her.

“He died in February,” she added.

“I’m sorry.”

“I don’t need it finished.”

“All right.”

“I just don’t want to be responsible for keeping it forever.”

Outside the office, a child asked someone why a displayed jigsaw puzzle was missing its sky.

Elias studied a tiny station drawn beside a river.

“Did your father leave notes?”

“Six boxes.”

“Ah.”

“That’s what I said.”

He offered her half the orange, which she accepted.

***

The museum had a procedure for donations. First came an interview. Then a period of consideration. Finally, if both parties agreed, the object entered the collection.

“What are you considering?” Mara asked.

“Whether we can care for it. Whether it belongs here. Whether you actually want to give it away.”

“And what am I considering?”

“Usually that last part.”

He led her upstairs to a room overlooking the abandoned platforms. Rain had begun to collect between the rails.

Here the exhibits were less tangible.

A pair of headphones played the opening of a symphony whose composer had become a dentist. A screen displayed the first eleven frames of an animated film. On a small table sat a telephone.

Its label said:

**A conversation rehearsed for nine years and never attempted.**

“Does it work?” Mara asked.

“The telephone? Yes.”

“What happens if you pick it up?”

“You hear a dial tone.”

“That’s all?”

“That has proved sufficient.”

At the far end of the room, a woman in a yellow cardigan was listening to the symphony. Her eyes were closed. When the recording stopped, she waited through the silence before pressing the button again.

“Do people come back often?” Mara asked.

“Some do.”

“To visit their things?”

“Sometimes other people’s.”

Mara watched the woman settle into the opening notes.

Her father had listened to the same radio program every Sunday while drawing. Mara could remember the announcer’s voice more clearly than she could remember his.

She resented the museum for making that possible to notice.

***

As a child, she had been allowed to name one town.

She chose Pancake.

Her father wrote it in pencil beside a small circle.

“Is it a large town?” he asked.

“Enormous.”

“How enormous?”

“A million people.”

He looked at the location she had selected, between a marsh and a quarry.

“They’ll need considerable infrastructure.”

She had been six. Infrastructure sounded like a species of insect.

The next weekend, Pancake had acquired a railway junction, three bridges, and a water-treatment plant. Her father explained that a million people could not simply be placed somewhere and left to manage.

At eleven, she asked him to change the name.

“To what?”

“Anything normal.”

He suggested Pancaster, and she agreed with relief.

By sixteen she found the whole enterprise mortifying. Other fathers built extensions, followed football, or became briefly interested in expensive bicycles. Hers spent evenings calculating freight traffic between places that did not exist.

“What’s the point?” she asked once.

He took off his glasses.

“I like to see where things go.”

She thought this evasive and said so.

Now she remembered that he had not argued. He had cleaned his glasses with the corner of his shirt and returned to the map.

When she unfolded it after his funeral, she found Pancaster where she remembered it.

In tiny lettering beneath the modern name he had added:

**Formerly Pancake.**

She had sat on the floor of his study for a long time, holding down the curling paper with both hands.

***

Elias suggested that she bring the boxes.

“Not necessarily to donate,” he said. “We have tables.”

The following Saturday, Mara arrived with a borrowed trolley and the grim efficiency she normally reserved for insurance claims.

The boxes contained notebooks, tracing paper, receipts, newspaper clippings, and envelopes covered in calculations. There were timetables for three competing rail companies. A folded sheet listed the changing population of Bellweather between 1840 and 1975.

“Good heavens,” Elias said.

“I did warn you.”

“This is a very unreliable railway.”

He showed her a timetable.

“The connection at East Mere is impossible.”

“Perhaps he made a mistake.”

“Perhaps. Or perhaps everyone in East Mere has been complaining about it for forty years.”

Mara almost smiled.

They sorted until lunchtime.

There were geological surveys, regional elections, two disputed borders, and a long-running argument concerning the placement of a municipal swimming pool. Nothing resembled a plot. There was no hidden manuscript, no grand revelation explaining why her father had needed this country.

Then she found a shopping list.

Eggs. Batteries. Apples. Ask Mara about Thursday.

On the reverse was a sketch of a harbor.

She remembered no particular Thursday. There had been hundreds.

For the first time since opening the boxes, she felt tired rather than determined.

Elias set down the notebook he was holding.

“There’s soup downstairs.”

“I should finish this box.”

“It’ll remain unfinished through lunch.”

She followed him reluctantly, carrying the shopping list in her pocket without having consciously decided to keep it.

***

Over soup, Mara asked how the museum had begun.

“With a woman called Agnes Vale,” Elias said. “She inherited an unfinished tapestry and couldn’t bear either to throw it away or to work on it.”

“So she founded a museum?”

“Not immediately. First she put it in a cupboard for thirty-two years.”

“That sounds more reasonable.”

“Then she rented this building.”

Agnes had been a civil engineer. The tapestry belonged to her mother. Its completed portion showed a garden, a fountain, and half a dog. Agnes remembered watching her mother stitch while listening to evening news reports. She could recall the color of the sewing basket and the click of the scissors.

She could not remember why her mother stopped.

“That bothered her,” Elias said. “There ought to have been an explanation. Illness, a quarrel, a shortage of thread. But perhaps she simply put it down one afternoon.”

“Did Agnes ever find out?”

“No.”

Mara stirred her soup.

“Is the tapestry here?”

“In storage. We rotate the collection.”

“Even the thing that started it?”

“The unfinished dog is vulnerable to light.”

He said this so plainly that Mara laughed again.

After lunch he showed her the conservation room, where two volunteers were building a support for a half-carved wooden bird.

No one appeared to be treating incompleteness as sacred. They dusted it, documented it, worried about insects. The place smelled of paper, glue, and the coffee someone had forgotten on a windowsill.

Mara found herself trusting it more because of that.

***

Near the bottom of the fourth box, she discovered an envelope marked WEST.

Inside were several sketches and a letter addressed to her.

She put the letter down immediately.

Elias, at the other end of the table, continued measuring a sheet of tracing paper.

“You can have the room,” he said.

“No. It’s fine.”

But he found an errand anyway.

The letter was undated.

Mara,

You asked once why I don’t finish the western side. I think I gave you a poor answer.

The difficulty is that I began at the eastern coast when you were small, and everything there has become rather settled. I know what the buildings look like. I know which roads flood. Adding anything feels less like inventing it than checking something I have forgotten.

The west is still different every time I look at it.

This probably does not explain much.

I thought you might like to draw some of it one day. No obligation. You would be entitled to improve the railway.

There was no farewell. Beneath the last sentence he had started a diagram of what appeared to be a suspension bridge.

Mara read the letter twice.

She wanted a more important letter, and then felt ashamed of wanting it. She wanted something that would account for the hospital, the missed calls, her impatience, his stubborn refusal to buy a safer ladder.

Instead, he had offered her an imaginary railway.

When Elias returned, she was studying the bridge.

“Tea?” he asked.

“Yes,” she said. “Please.”

***

Mara returned the next week, and the week after that.

She did not draw the western districts.

Instead, she catalogued what existed. She entered place names into a spreadsheet. She learned that Saint Venn had lost its saint during a brief republican period, then restored him because replacing the road signs had proved expensive.

She found three versions of the disputed swimming pool.

She discovered that Pancaster’s astonishing growth had eventually slowed, though it remained an important industrial center.

Occasionally she was angry with him. The country had received an attention that his gutters, blood pressure, and friendships could have used. There were afternoons when every careful contour line seemed evidence of misplaced effort.

On those days she closed the boxes early.

One rainy Saturday, the elderly woman whose husband had made the chair sat beside her.

“Any progress?”

“On sorting it.”

“That counts.”

“Did you ever want to fix the chair?”

“Certainly. I wanted him to fix it.”

“Afterward, I mean.”

The woman considered this.

“For a while. Then I bought a chair.”

Mara laughed.

“I’m serious,” the woman said. “I needed somewhere to sit. That one wasn’t going to become useful just because I missed him.”

They watched rain running down the windows.

“What do you think I should do with all this?” Mara asked.

“I couldn’t possibly know.”

It was, Mara thought, the kindest answer anyone had given her in months.

The woman took out a crossword and asked whether she knew a seven-letter word for a river mouth.

***

In September, the museum accepted the map and five of the six boxes.

Mara kept the letter, the shopping list, and a notebook containing small sketches she particularly liked. She also kept a duplicated railway timetable, partly because Elias had become unreasonable about the East Mere connection.

The map required a large case in the departures hall.

Together they wrote the label:

**A country developed over twenty-three years by Daniel Vale, drainage inspector. The western districts remain undetermined.**

“You’re related to Agnes?” Elias asked, seeing the name on the form.

“No.”

“People will ask.”

“They can ask.”

On opening day, a boy pressed his hands against the glass.

“Why didn’t he finish it?”

Mara, standing nearby, considered several answers.

“He liked working on it,” she said.

The boy accepted this more readily than she expected. He followed the railway with one finger held just above the glass.

“That train should go over there.”

“Yes,” she said. “It probably should.”

Before leaving, she went upstairs and picked up the telephone.

The dial tone was ordinary and faintly harsh.

She held the receiver for a minute. She did not imagine an answer. Then she put it back, thanked Elias, and walked outside.

A bus was waiting at the stop across the road.

Mara could take it home, or walk along the river and buy something for dinner. She checked the sky. The rain seemed finished for the afternoon.

She chose the river.

Behind her, the museum clock continued to offer its single, useless piece of information.
